title: 🧥 Nvidia loses its leather jacket
body_text: Happy Monday to everyone except those whose employers use Microsoft Outlook for email. Those poor souls, who already spend half their workday searching for emails that are definitely in their inboxes, got an unexpected break on Thursday and Friday thanks to a widespread Microsoft outage . They probably needed it. After all, Teams tells their bosses they're slacking off if they leave their mouse untouched for more than five minutes. Headlines last week were dominated by one thing. For those living under a rock, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following a series of bombshell reports that painted a picture of a leather jacket-clad man who founded a chip company for video games, became one of the most powerful people in the world, and apparently succumbed to the temptations that came with it. First came reports that Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman who US intelligence officials reportedly considered a spy for the Chinese government. The woman’s company, Megaspeed, was reportedly able to obtain Nvidia chips in China despite export controls designed to prevent China from beating the US on artificial intelligence. (Oh, and during this time, he was also reportedly having affairs with at least two Nvidia employees.) Meanwhile, in Washington, they’re all trying to find the guy who was supposed to prevent this from happening but didn’t. Lawmakers called on Haung and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify. This brings into question how long Lutnick, who is supposed to be in charge of enforcing those export controls, will stay with the administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he supported blacklisting Megaspeed but Lutnick didn’t act . Secretary of State Marco Rubio (a Republican presidential hopeful), also reportedly sounded the alarms about the relationship to no avail . Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will be interim CEO. But the transition could be awkward, given that Huang didn't always seem to hold her in particularly high regard. As recently as this summer, Huang belittled her at a meeting and called her a “deer in the headlights,” according to The Wall Street Journal . When asked earlier this fall by Wired who the most powerful women in tech were, Huang did not name her. We still don’t know who will replace Huang on a permanent basis. President Trump suggested former Apple CEO, Tim Cook. Prediction markets are favoring Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing. The stock has taken a massive hit from the scandal. Nvidia is still scheduled to report earnings results on Tuesday, in which it may report better-than-expected numbers, as it often does, which could potentially offer some relief. Kress will take questions from analysts, some of whom downgraded the stock this week . The market is still figuring out how to price in this juicy gossip. On one hand, the scandal shows people want Nvidia's chips so badly that they're willing to (allegedly) commit espionage to get them. And demand for those chips isn't going to disappear just because Huang is gone. On the other hand, the allegations have invited a major legal and regulatory headache for Nvidia at a time investors have been jittery about the AI trade and the public opinion on AI infrastructure has soured. Then there's the Jensen factor. Maybe Huang, the only CEO the company has ever had, has the secret sauce that a successor won't be able to replicate. As my colleague Luke Kawa points out in the EntryPoint newsletter, Huang's interpersonal skills helped bolster demand (perhaps to a fault). The question now is whether Nvidia's next CEO can keep the orders flowing without the industry's most recognizable salesman. As the Nvidia scandal unfolded Thursday, the chip company completely dominated trading activity on Robinhood. 6,184 single stocks were traded on Robinhood Markets on Thursday, and net purchases of Nvidia were more than double the rest of those 6,183 stocks, combined! title: 🥀 Jensen Huang’s remarkable ouster
body_text: It took several hours longer than expected, but the SS United States is now sitting at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico just off the Florida coast near Pensacola. Rather than serving meals of caviar and roast duck as it did during its heyday zipping across the Atlantic, it will now form an artificial reef that attracts marlin and swordfish, and eventually with them, divers and fishermen, the Associated Press reports . The SS US was larger than the Titanic and set a transatlantic speed record on its first voyage in 1952 with an average speed of 41 miles per hour. Federal rules prevent the use of explosives in intentional scuttlings, so instead Coleen Marine, the company tasked with the sinking, removed the tanks that held seawater used to cool the ship’s boilers. Once water flowed in through the intakes, it flooded the vessel. Over 400 portholes were also removed and large holes cut into the deck. The SS US joins more than 500 other artificial reefs in the area off the Gulf coast where it now lays. Stocks fell on Thursday as Nvidia fell before recovering much of its losses and the AI trade showed resilience despite the ouster of one of the most important CEOs in the industry. In a turn of events that would have been shocking even a week ago, Jensen Huang is out as the CEO of Nvidia after his position leading the most important chipmaker in the world became untenable following the development of a series of scandals about his conduct. The move comes at a major inflection point in the AI trade, after several months of the biggest names from Intel to the AI labs to the neoclouds being rattled by earnings, the debt market, and somewhat ambiguous vibes around the ultimate value of this technology and the ultimate ability of the companies involved in the AI trade to capture it. Huang had long been the sector’s biggest cheerleader, its financier, and the guy responsible for selling the single most valuable piece of hardware technology in the whole boom. The coming weeks will reveal precisely how necessary Huang is to the action here. Consider it a fundamental test of the “great man theory of history” as it applies to business. Was Nvidia successful because of Huang’s particular vision and networking ability? Or will Nvidia be able to continue its run absent its leather-jacketed leader, because at this point it’s not exactly rocket science selling a GPU to a data center. The manner of Huang’s departure will at the very least likely be bruising for Nvidia in the short- to medium-term; the scandal began when it was reported that Huang was engaged in a romantic entanglement with a woman who had been identified as a likely Chinese intelligence asset. The incident that precipitated his actual departure — reporting that indicated this sort of behavior was not exactly exceptional, and that Huang had allegedly been involved with co-workers too — doesn’t exactly paint a great picture. Either way, now Congress is getting involved , as House investigators tend to hate it when the businessman behind the single most important piece of technology of the decade gets honeypotted by America’s primary geopolitical and industrial rival. Nvidia shares took it on the chin this week, but retail traders appear to be bullish on the company’s ability to perform well absent Huang. According to my colleague Luke Kawa and the EntryPoint newsletter , traders have been enthusiastically buying the dip here in anticipation that, however things shake out with Huang, people are going to need those graphics cards and they’re probably fine buying them from Colette Kress for the time being. Indeed, one plausible fallout of this stands to benefit the large firms helming the AI industry in the United States. The frontier labs have long argued that tough regulation of AI, especially the open-source AI that dominates China’s role in the emerging tech, is a necessity. Huang opposed that, through his desire to export his chips to whoever would buy them and his support of the open source world of models and his purchase of HuggingFace. title: 🍿 Boxd clever
body_text: A tidbit for anyone somehow still unconvinced by the Power of the Pod in 2026: Winning congressional candidates at this year’s midterms made almost three times as many podcast appearances as their unsuccessful counterparts. According to Spotify data shared with Axios , a whopping ~83% of House and Senate candidates made at least one appearance on a stand-alone pod (not TV news programs clipped up and redistributed as podcasts) across the cycle. Huge shout-out to friend of the show(s) Democrat Rep. Ro Khanna who managed to make 242 appearances on 175 shows from January 1, 2025, through November 3, 2026, per Spotify’s podcast figures. Stocks gained on Wednesday as tech stocks rallied after CoreWeave vaulted almost 25% after the neocloud beat Wall Street revenue estimates and gave guidance ahead of analyst expectations. Just a couple of months or so after a Times piece broke the news that Letterboxd — a social media network where ~30 million users log and review movies they’ve watched — had been attracting takeover interest from a host of names in the entertainment industry, it seems that the Grey Lady herself is now leading the charge. Last week, the NYT reported that its parent company had entered into advanced talks to buy the platform for around $330 million. Letterboxd reps and The New York Times Company chose to take non-speaking roles in the report, though sources close to the discussions were on hand to add color. Apparently, Sony Pictures and ever-popular artsy production house A24 had both been circling the platform, with the latter dropping out as the potential takeover bids rose. For its part in the now exclusive negotiations, the Times Company has reportedly discussed keeping Matthew Buchanan and Karl von Randow at the helm, the pair having launched Letterboxd together at a Brooklyn web conference in 2011 . At the time, the final installment in the Harry Potter movie franchise was topping the box office. The media landscape has changed a bit since. For instance, never has the artist’s eternal “everyone’s a critic” complaint been truer, as platforms like Letterboxd and the Amazon -owned Goodreads have almost gamified art consumption; films are something to log, books are something to shelve. Just looking at Letterboxd’s analytics gives you a decent picture of how the business of letting cinephiles record and review their latest watches has boomed in recent years. Given how user figures have ballooned since the pandemic era, with each metric in Letterboxd’s annual year-end review rising at least four times from 2020 to 2025, it’s little wonder that some within the industry have started to refer to younger fervent film fans as the “ Letterboxd Generation .” The rising popularity of platform features such as “ Four Favorites ,” now a mainstay question for celebs stopped on red carpets and stuck in press junkets, as well as getting one of the biggest names in media onboard, makes it hard to imagine a world where Letterboxd users aren’t logging 1 billion+ movies on the platform each year at some point in the near future. As The New York Times Company’s metamorphosis from a news peddler to games-entertainment-product reviews-and-recipes behemoth that runs a side gig sending reporters to war zones continues, deals like this only make more sense. In fairness, the company behind America’s paper of record has provided much more than the news for a while now, having long realized that it needs more than straight reporting to keep modern audiences engaged (and paying up) in the digital age. Indeed, just like Letterboxd hopes that the financial backing and increased visibility from any potential sale will help juice their user numbers and boost its revenue, the Times likely views the Letterboxd deal — like the acquisitions of Wordle and The Athletic before it — as another potential stepping stone towards its goal to 15 million subscribers by the end of 2027. 🏈 NFL: It’s an NFC East showdown tonight between the Washington Commanders and the New York Giants, with New York a 57% favorite .
